messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 19
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: Oceania
  relationship_status: In a relationship
  occupation: Fisherman
  trauma_type: Witnessed other trauma
  pcl5: 49

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Transportation (Bicycle): Bicycle, Auditory (Footsteps): Footsteps behind or nearby, Auditory (Sounds): Related sounds
  Maladaptive Strategies: Overwork: work excessively to avoid being alone with thoughts, Avoid Sex: Sex, Screen Escape: I spend long hours on my phone, games, or internet to avoid thinking
  Threat: Body Reacts Before Mind: My body reacts to danger before I have even had time to think, Concentration: Having difficulty concentrating, Threat in Delays: When something takes longer than expected I assume something bad is happening
  Memory: Emotion Without Image: Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory, Guilt on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense guilt, Uncontrolled Access: The memory forces its way into my mind when I do not want it to
  Negative Appraisals: Fear of Rage: I will not be able to control my anger and will do something terrible, Failed to Protect: I should have protected others and I failed, Body as Enemy: My body keeps reacting as if I am still in danger even when I am safe

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Malia was 19, a young woman from an Oceania background living in a small coastal community, and she had been trying to keep up with work as a fisherman while staying in a relationship that mattered deeply to her. The event that changed things happened at dusk on the wharf, when she and a few others were unloading gear and a friend slipped near the water, hitting the edge hard before disappearing below the surface in a moment of chaos. Malia had seen enough to know something was terribly wrong, but not enough to feel she could make it right, and that helpless gap has stayed with her. In the months since, she has found that a bicycle coming up behind her on the road, footsteps close on the dock, or the sharp, related sounds of the wharf can catch her body before her mind has time to catch up. Her heart jumps, her muscles brace, and she feels danger arriving in her body first; when something is taking longer than expected, she immediately assumes something bad is happening, as if delay itself means another loss.

Those moments do not just startle her; they pull at the memory of that evening. Sometimes Malia is hit by the full emotional force of it without any clear picture at all, a wave of panic, dread, and guilt that seems to come from nowhere. At other times the memory forces its way in when she does not want it to, and with it comes the conviction that she should have protected the others and failed. She becomes especially troubled by the thought that her body keeps reacting as if she is still in danger even when she is safe, which makes her fear that she is damaged in some permanent way. The memory and the appraisal feed one another: the more the scene intrudes, the more certain she becomes that she did not do enough, and the more she blames herself, the more the event returns with the same awful emotional force. Even the triggers become loaded with that judgment; a bicycle near her home, footsteps behind her in the market, or a sudden sound on the pier can feel like proof that danger is close again and that she has already failed once before. What frightens her most is not only the memory itself but the fear of her own rage, because when her body goes rigid and her mind jumps ahead to catastrophe, she worries she will not be able to control her anger and do something terrible.

To keep this from happening, Malia has built a life of constant diversion. She works excessively on boats and around the harbor so she does not have to sit alone with her thoughts, and when she is off duty she can lose long hours on her phone, games, or the internet to keep her mind occupied. She has also been avoiding sex with her partner, partly because being physically close makes her feel too exposed and partly because she is afraid that if she lets herself settle, the memory will come flooding back. These strategies have given her short stretches of relief, but they have also made the rest of the pattern harder to escape. Overwork leaves her exhausted and less able to concentrate, which makes ordinary tasks feel even more threatening; if a meeting runs late or a text is unanswered, she assumes something bad is happening and scans for danger. The screen time and constant busyness also make the memory more likely to ambush her when she finally slows down, because the moment she is alone, the event rushes in with the same guilt and fear. Since she is always trying to outrun those feelings, even the familiar sounds of the dock and the feel of a bicycle passing close by have become sharper, more charged cues that pull her back into the same state of alarm. Her boyfriend has noticed that she is present in body but distant in conversation, and that she seems to be living around the event rather than beyond it.

Malia came for help now because she is tired of feeling as if every delay, every footstep behind her, and every passing sound might be the start of another disaster. She wants to be able to work on the water without bracing for catastrophe, to stay with her partner without pulling away, and to believe that her body is not betraying her. More than anything, she is hoping to stop the memory from taking over her life and to find a way to live without the constant fear that she will fail again or lose control of herself.
